header:
How to check and fix
your credit report

lines.text: 1 in 5 had credit report errors. Is yours?
lines.say: One in five had credit report errors. Is yours?

lines.text: Checking takes one free website. Fixing an error often starts with one letter. Here's the whole process.
lines.say: Checking takes one free website, and fixing an error often starts with one letter. Here's the whole process, step by step.

lines.text: That 1 in 5 comes from a Federal Trade Commission study released in 2013. About 1,000 people went through their reports.
lines.say: That one in five comes from a Federal Trade Commission study released in twenty thirteen. About a thousand people went through their reports with help.

lines.text: And 5% had errors serious enough that they could pay more for things like car loans and insurance.
lines.say: And five percent had errors serious enough that they could end up paying more for things like car loans and insurance.

lines.text: Now, a credit report isn't your credit score. The report is the raw file. The score is just a number built from it.
lines.say: Now, a credit report isn't your credit score. The report is the raw file. The score is just a number that gets built from it.

lines.text: Garbage in, garbage out.
lines.say: Garbage in, garbage out.

lines.text: So here's the plan: get the reports, read them, dispute what's wrong, and protect the file.
lines.say: So here's the plan: get the reports, read them line by line, dispute what's wrong, and then protect the file.

lines.text: Rules here come from the FTC, the CFPB and federal law. This is education, not advice.
lines.say: The rules here come from the F T C, the C F P B and federal law. This is education, not advice.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Get all three reports
lines.say: Chapter one: get all three reports.

lines.text: There are three big credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Each keeps its own file on you.
lines.say: There are three big credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Each one keeps its own separate file on you.

lines.text: They're not identical. Not every lender reports to all three, so one file can be missing something.
lines.say: And they're not identical. Not every lender reports to all three, so one file can be missing something the others have.

lines.text: The official place to get them free is AnnualCreditReport.com.
lines.say: The official place to get them for free is Annual Credit Report dot com.

lines.text: It's the only site federal law authorizes for free reports. Look-alike sites may try to sell you something.
lines.say: It's the only site federal law authorizes for free reports. Look-alike sites with similar names may try to sell you something.

lines.text: You used to get one free report a year from each bureau. That changed.
lines.say: You used to get one free report a year from each bureau. That changed.

lines.text: Free weekly reports started during the pandemic, and in 2023 the bureaus made them permanent.
lines.say: Free weekly reports started during the pandemic, and in twenty twenty-three the bureaus made them permanent.

lines.text: So that's 3 bureaus, every week, for $0.
lines.say: So that's three bureaus, every single week, for zero dollars.

lines.text: Two things to know. The free report doesn't include your score. It's just the file.
lines.say: Two things to know. First, the free report doesn't include your credit score. It's just the file itself.

lines.text: And checking your own report has no score hit. None. A loan application is a hard inquiry; your own look isn't.
lines.say: And second, checking your own report has no score hit. None. A loan application is a hard inquiry, but your own look isn't.

lines.text: You can also request reports by phone at 1-877-322-8228, if online isn't your thing.
lines.say: You can also request them by phone at one, eight seven seven, three two two, eight two two eight, if online isn't your thing.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Read it line by line
lines.say: Chapter two: read it line by line.

lines.text: Open one report and go section by section. Start with the boring part: your personal info.
lines.say: Open one report and go section by section. Start with the boring part, which is your personal information.

lines.text: Check your name, addresses, and Social Security digits. Someone else's info can mean a mixed file.
lines.say: Check your name, your addresses, and the Social Security digits. Someone else's info in there can mean a mixed-up file.

lines.text: Next, the accounts. Do you recognize every single one?
lines.say: Next, the accounts. Do you recognize every single one of them?

lines.text: An account you never opened is a red flag for identity theft, not just a typo.
lines.say: An account you never opened is a red flag for identity theft, not just a typo.

lines.text: Then check each account's status. A closed account shown as open, or a debt listed twice, is an error.
lines.say: Then check each account's status. A closed account shown as open, or one debt listed twice, is an error.

lines.text: Now the balances and credit limits. This is where a small error can cost you.
lines.say: Now look at the balances and credit limits. This is where a small error can quietly cost you.

lines.text: Why? In FICO's formula, amounts owed make up about 30% of the score. Payment history is 35%.
lines.say: Why? In FICO's formula, amounts owed make up about thirty percent of the score, and payment history makes up about thirty-five percent.

lines.text: Here's a worked example. It's our math, with made-up numbers.
lines.say: Here's a worked example. This is our math, with made-up numbers.

lines.text: You have two cards. Card A has a $3,000 limit, Card B a $2,000 limit. That's $5,000 total.
lines.say: Say you have two cards. Card A has a three thousand dollar limit, and Card B has a two thousand dollar limit. That's five thousand dollars total.

lines.text: You really owe $600 on Card A and $400 on Card B. That's $1,000.
lines.say: You really owe six hundred dollars on Card A and four hundred on Card B. That's one thousand dollars.

lines.text: $1,000 divided by $5,000 is 20%. That's your utilization, the share of your limits you're using.
lines.say: One thousand divided by five thousand is twenty percent. That's your utilization, the share of your limits you're using.

lines.text: But the report still shows Card B at an old balance of $1,400, from before you paid it down.
lines.say: But the report still shows Card B at an old balance of fourteen hundred dollars, from before you paid it down.

lines.text: Now it's $600 plus $1,400, which is $2,000. Divided by $5,000, that's 40%.
lines.say: Now it's six hundred plus fourteen hundred, which is two thousand dollars. Divided by five thousand, that's forty percent.

lines.text: One wrong number doubled how much of your credit you look like you're using.
lines.say: One wrong number doubled how much of your credit you look like you're using.

lines.text: Last, check late marks and inquiries. A 30-day late you didn't earn, or a loan you never applied for.
lines.say: Last, check late payment marks and inquiries. Look for a thirty-day late you didn't earn, or a loan application you never made.

lines.text: Write down every problem, and which bureau's report it's on. You'll need that list in chapter 4.
lines.say: Write down every problem, and which bureau's report it's on. You'll need that list in chapter four.

lines.text: Chapter 3: How common are errors?
lines.say: Chapter three: how common are errors, really?

lines.text: Back to that FTC study. It looked at 2,968 credit reports from 1,001 people.
lines.say: Back to that F T C study. It looked at two thousand nine hundred sixty-eight credit reports from one thousand and one people.

lines.text: After fixes, about 1 in 10 people saw their score change.
lines.say: After the fixes, about one in ten people saw their score change.

lines.text: And about 1 in 20 saw a change of more than 25 points. That can mean real money on a loan rate.
lines.say: And about one in twenty saw their score move by more than twenty-five points. That can mean real money on a loan rate.

lines.text: That study is old, so here's newer data: complaints to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
lines.say: That study is getting old, so here's newer data: complaints sent to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

lines.text: In 2020, the CFPB got about 540,000 complaints (0.54M). By 2025 it was about 6.6 million, per its annual reports.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, the C F P B received about five hundred forty thousand complaints. By twenty twenty-five, it was about six point six million, according to its annual reports.

lines.text: That's more than double 2024's 3.2 million, in a single year.
lines.say: That's more than double twenty twenty-four's three point two million, in a single year.

lines.text: And more than 5.8 million of the 2025 complaints were about credit or consumer reporting.
lines.say: And more than five point eight million of the twenty twenty-five complaints were about credit or consumer reporting.

lines.text: That's about 88% of everything people complained about.
lines.say: That's about eighty-eight percent of everything people complained about.

lines.text: A fair caveat: a complaint isn't proof of an error. In June 2026, the CFPB said third parties and high-volume filing may make the data less reliable. Consumer groups disagreed.
lines.say: A fair caveat: a complaint isn't proof of an error. In June twenty twenty-six, the C F P B said third parties and high-volume filing may make the data less reliable. Consumer groups disagreed.

lines.text: Either way, the lesson is the same. Nobody checks your file for you. You do.
lines.say: Either way, the lesson is the same. Nobody checks your file for you. You do.

lines.text: Chapter 4: File the dispute
lines.say: Chapter four: file the dispute.

lines.text: Disputes are free. You file with each bureau whose report shows the error, online, by mail, or by phone.
lines.say: Disputes are free. You file with each bureau whose report shows the error, online, by mail, or by phone.

lines.text: Online is fastest. Mail gives you a paper trail. Either way, your evidence matters most.
lines.say: Online is usually the fastest. Mail gives you a paper trail. Either way, it's your evidence that matters most.

lines.text: The FTC says a dispute letter should include your full name and address.
lines.say: The F T C says a dispute letter should include your full name and address.

lines.text: Then list each item you're disputing, with the account number.
lines.say: Then list each item you're disputing, along with the account number.

lines.text: Explain why it's wrong, and ask for it to be corrected or deleted.
lines.say: Explain why each one is wrong, and ask for it to be corrected or deleted.

lines.text: And attach copies, never originals, of proof: statements, payment confirmations, letters.
lines.say: And attach copies, never originals, of your proof: statements, payment confirmations, letters.

lines.text: In our example, that's the bank statement showing Card B paid down to $400.
lines.say: In our example, that's the bank statement showing Card B paid down to four hundred dollars.

lines.text: Here's the part most people skip: also dispute with the furnisher.
lines.say: Now here's the part most people skip: also dispute directly with the furnisher.

lines.text: The bureau stores the data. The furnisher, the lender or collector, sends it. The FTC says you can dispute with both.
lines.say: The bureau stores the data. The furnisher, meaning the lender or collector, is the one that sends it. The F T C says you can dispute with both, using the same documents.

lines.text: Fix it at the source, and the lender has to correct it with every bureau it reports to.
lines.say: Fix it at the source, and the lender has to correct it with every bureau it reports to.

lines.text: Now the clock. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bureau has to pass your dispute to the furnisher, within 5 business days.
lines.say: Now the clock. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the bureau has to pass your dispute along to the furnisher within five business days.

lines.text: The bureau generally has 30 days to investigate.
lines.say: The bureau generally has thirty days to investigate.

lines.text: That can stretch to 45 days if you send new information during the window, or for some disputes after a free annual report.
lines.say: That can stretch to forty-five days if you send new information during the window, or for some disputes filed after a free annual report.

lines.text: Then it has 5 business days to send you the results, plus a free copy of the report if it changed.
lines.say: After that, it has five business days to send you the results, plus a free copy of your report if it changed.

lines.text: If the info is wrong, or can't be verified, it has to be corrected or deleted.
lines.say: If the information is wrong, or it can't be verified, it has to be corrected or deleted.

lines.text: Keep copies of everything, with dates. Treat it like a little court case, because it might become one.
lines.say: Keep copies of everything, with the dates. Treat it like a little court case, because it might turn into one.

lines.text: Now, what if the bureau says no?
lines.say: Now, what happens if the bureau looks at your dispute and says no?

lines.text: It happens. The bureau says the item is verified, and you still know it's wrong. You have options.
lines.say: Sometimes the bureau says the item is verified, and you still know it's wrong. You have options.

lines.text: First, you can add a statement of dispute to your file. Federal law says the bureau can cap it at 100 words.
lines.say: First, you can add a statement of dispute to your file. Federal law says the bureau can cap it at one hundred words.

lines.text: The exact text: the agency "may limit such statements to not more than one hundred words" if it helps you write a clear summary.
lines.say: Here's the exact text: the agency may limit such statements to not more than one hundred words, if it helps you write a clear summary.

scene.text: May limit such statements to not more than one hundred words.

lines.text: After that, the bureau generally has to flag the item as disputed in future reports, so lenders can see your side.
lines.say: After that, the bureau generally has to flag the item as disputed in future reports, so lenders can see your side.

lines.text: Second, dispute again with new evidence, and go straight to the furnisher if you haven't.
lines.say: Second, dispute again with any new evidence, and go straight to the furnisher if you haven't yet.

lines.text: Third, you can file a complaint with the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov. The company is asked to respond.
lines.say: Third, you can file a complaint with the C F P B at consumer finance dot gov, and the company is asked to respond.

lines.text: You can also contact your state attorney general. And the law gives you the right to sue over violations.
lines.say: You can also contact your state attorney general. And the law gives you the right to sue if your rights are violated.

lines.text: Most disputes never get that far. But knowing the next step keeps you calm.
lines.say: Most disputes never get that far. But knowing the next step keeps you calm.

lines.text: Chapter 5: What stays, and for how long
lines.say: Chapter five: what stays, and for how long.

lines.text: Here's the hard truth. You can only remove errors. Accurate bad news stays, for a while.
lines.say: Here's the hard truth. You can only remove errors. Accurate bad news stays, at least for a while.

lines.text: Hard inquiries, from applying for credit, can stay up to 2 years.
lines.say: Hard inquiries, from applying for credit, can stay on your report for up to two years.

lines.text: Most negative items, like late payments and collections, can be reported for up to 7 years.
lines.say: Most negative items, like late payments and collections, can generally be reported for up to seven years.

lines.text: And a Chapter 7 bankruptcy can stay up to 10 years from the filing date.
lines.say: And a Chapter Seven bankruptcy can stay for up to ten years from the filing date.

lines.text: So anyone promising to erase accurate, recent history for a fee is promising something the law doesn't allow.
lines.say: So anyone promising to erase accurate, recent history for a fee is promising something the law doesn't allow.

lines.text: In fact, the FTC says it's illegal for credit repair companies to charge you before they do the work.
lines.say: In fact, the F T C says it's illegal for credit repair companies to charge you before they've actually done the work.

lines.text: Now, protecting the file. The strongest tool is a credit freeze, and it's been free by law since 2018.
lines.say: Now, protecting the file. The strongest tool is a credit freeze, and it's been free by federal law since twenty eighteen.

lines.text: A freeze blocks new lenders from pulling your file, which makes new credit in your name much harder to open. It doesn't change your score.
lines.say: A freeze blocks new lenders from pulling your file, which makes new credit in your name much harder to open. It doesn't change your score.

lines.text: You set it up with each of the 3 bureaus, and lift it before you apply for a loan.
lines.say: You set it up separately with each of the three bureaus, and you lift it before you apply for a loan.

lines.text: A lighter option is a fraud alert. An initial alert is free, lasts 1 year, and one bureau tells the other two.
lines.say: A lighter option is a fraud alert. An initial alert is free, it lasts one year, and the bureau you contact tells the other two.

lines.text: Identity theft victims with a report from IdentityTheft.gov can get an extended alert for 7 years.
lines.say: Identity theft victims with a report from Identity Theft dot gov can get an extended alert that lasts seven years.

lines.text: Lenders must take extra steps to confirm it's you. You can still apply for credit.
lines.say: With an alert, lenders have to take extra steps to confirm it's really you. You can still apply for credit.

lines.text: Before the recap, the common mistakes. Number one: checking only one bureau.
lines.say: Before the recap, let's hit the common mistakes. Number one: checking only one bureau.

lines.text: Two: using a look-alike site instead of AnnualCreditReport.com.
lines.say: Two: using a look-alike site instead of Annual Credit Report dot com.

lines.text: Three: mailing your only copy of the proof.
lines.say: Three: mailing off your only copy of the proof.

lines.text: Four: disputing with the bureau but never telling the lender that sent the bad data.
lines.say: Four: disputing with the bureau, but never telling the lender that sent the bad data.

lines.text: And a bonus: forgetting to lift a freeze before a loan application, then wondering why it got stuck.
lines.say: And a bonus one: forgetting to lift a freeze before a loan application, and then wondering why it got stuck.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The one-screen checklist
lines.say: Chapter six: the one-screen checklist.

lines.text: One: pull all 3 reports free at AnnualCreditReport.com. Weekly is allowed.
lines.say: One: pull all three reports for free at Annual Credit Report dot com. You're allowed to do it weekly.

lines.text: Two: check names, accounts, balances, limits, late marks and inquiries.
lines.say: Two: check the names, accounts, balances, limits, late marks and inquiries.

lines.text: Three: dispute errors with the bureau and the furnisher, with copies of proof. Expect about 30 days.
lines.say: Three: dispute errors with the bureau and the furnisher, with copies of proof. Expect about thirty days.

lines.text: Four: if you need it, freeze your credit at all 3 bureaus for free.
lines.say: Four: if you need it, freeze your credit at all three bureaus, for free.

lines.text: Remember the FTC's 1 in 5. The odds you'll find something are not small.
lines.say: Remember the F T C's one in five. The odds that you'll find something are not small.

lines.text: And in our example, one stale balance made 20% look like 40%. Fixing it started with one letter.
lines.say: And in our example, one stale balance made twenty percent look like forty percent. Fixing it started with one letter.

lines.text: Your credit report is your money's résumé. A little time to proofread it is a pretty good deal.
lines.say: Your credit report is basically your money's resume. A little time to proofread it is a pretty good deal.

post.title: How to Check and Fix Your Credit Report: 1 in 5 Found an Error
post.ig: 1 in 5 people in an FTC study found an error on a credit report. Here's how to check yours and fix it, free.
post.tiktok: Your credit report might be wrong. 1 in 5 people in an FTC study found an error. Here's the fix.
post.yt_desc:
In a Federal Trade Commission study published in 2013, 1 in 5 people found an error on at least one of their three credit reports. This guide walks through every step: getting free weekly reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion at AnnualCreditReport.com (made permanent in 2023), what to check line by line, and a worked example (our math) showing how one stale balance turns 20% utilization into 40%. We cover how to dispute with the bureau and the furnisher, the 30-day (sometimes 45-day) investigation clock under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, how long negative items stay (7 years for most, 10 for Chapter 7 bankruptcy), free credit freezes (since 2018), fraud alerts, and what to do if a dispute fails. We also chart CFPB complaints from 2020 to 2025.

CHAPTERS

Sources: FTC, Report to Congress on credit report accuracy (Dec 2012; press release Feb 11, 2013); CFPB Consumer Response Annual Reports 2020-2025 (latest Mar 31, 2026); CFPB complaint system announcement (June 24, 2026); National Consumer Law Center comments (2026); FTC consumer alert on permanent free weekly credit reports (Oct 13, 2023); FTC, Disputing Errors on Your Credit Reports; FTC, Free credit freezes are here (Sept 2018) and Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts; CFPB, Ask CFPB on dispute timelines and negative information; Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681i; myFICO, What's in my FICO Scores; Experian.

News and education, not financial advice.
